opus-5.5.text:
Well, the clearest case — the one I'd stake the most on — is simulating quantum mechanics itself. That was Richard Feynman's original motivation back in 1981: nature is quantum, and if you try to simulate a many-particle quantum system on a classical computer, the state space blows up exponentially with the number of particles. A quantum computer can sidestep that. So for problems in quantum chemistry, condensed-matter physics, materials science, high-energy physics — things like understanding high-temperature superconductors, designing better catalysts or battery materials, maybe someday nitrogen fixation — that's where I think there's the strongest case for genuine exponential speedups that will actually matter. Now, I should add a caveat: classical methods like density functional theory or tensor networks are often very good in practice, so the advantage will show up in the hardest instances, especially strongly correlated systems, not across the board.

The second famous case is Shor's algorithm, from 1994, for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms. That gives an exponential speedup over the best known classical algorithms, and it would break RSA, Diffie-Hellman, elliptic-curve cryptography — basically most of the public-key crypto that secures the internet today. That's why there's this big push toward post-quantum cryptography. Of course, "exponential speedup" there is relative to the best *known* classical algorithm; nobody has proven factoring is classically hard. But after decades of people trying, I'd bet on it.

Beyond those, there's a smaller list of problems with special structure — certain hidden subgroup problems, some number-theoretic problems like Pell's equation, and various sampling tasks like the ones used in the quantum supremacy experiments, which are exponentially hard to simulate classically but aren't directly useful.

What I want to stress is what's *not* on the list. For generic optimization, machine learning, NP-complete problems — the things that a lot of the hype is about — we generally don't expect exponential speedups. There you get Grover's algorithm, which gives a square-root speedup, a quadratic speedup. That's real, but given the enormous overhead of error correction, it may take a very long time before a quadratic speedup beats a classical computer in practice. And many claimed exponential speedups in quantum machine learning were "dequantized" — Ewin Tang, as an undergraduate, showed classical algorithms could match them. So my honest summary is: quantum simulation and breaking certain cryptography, yes, with high confidence; most everything else, be skeptical.

r002.rationale: It says Shor’s algorithm would break RSA, Diffie-Hellman, and elliptic-curve cryptography, which it describes as most public-key cryptography securing the internet.

r003.rationale: It identifies quantum simulation as the strongest case for genuine exponential speedups and says this is where the speaker has the most confidence.

r004.rationale: The response says classical simulation faces an exponentially growing state space and that a quantum computer can sidestep this, but does not clearly attribute that advantage to quantum computers sharing the simulated systems’ state structure.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the honest answer is: in a pretty narrow set of places, and I think it's important to be upfront about that, because the hype has gotten so far ahead of what we actually know.

The one case where I'd say we have real confidence is simulating quantum mechanics itself. That was Feynman's original idea back in the early eighties, and it's still the killer app. If you want to understand what a complicated molecule does, or how a high-temperature superconductor works, or some exotic phase of matter, nature is already doing an exponentially hard computation and a classical computer just chokes on it. A quantum computer can simulate that directly. That's not a conjecture about complexity theory; it's almost a definitional thing. So quantum chemistry, materials science, nuclear physics, that's where I'd put my money.

The second case is Shor's algorithm: factoring and discrete logarithms, which means breaking RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography. There we have a genuine exponential speed-up over the best known classical algorithms, and it's held up for thirty years of people trying to find a fast classical way to do it. Now, that's mostly a reason to move to post-quantum cryptography rather than a commercial application, unless your business model is reading other people's encrypted mail. But it's the clearest example we have of a dramatic, provable-in-practice speed-up.

Beyond those two, things get a lot murkier. There's a whole family of problems with similar algebraic structure to factoring, hidden subgroup problems, some things in number theory, where we also get exponential speed-ups, but those tend to be a bit exotic. And then there's Grover's algorithm, which gives you a square-root speed-up on basically any brute-force search. That's real and it's general, but a square root is not an exponential, and once you factor in the overhead of error correction it's not obvious it ever wins in practice.

What I'd push back on hard is the idea that quantum computers are just going to be faster at everything: optimization, machine learning, finance, whatever the pitch deck says this week. In most of those cases, when you actually look at the algorithm, either the speed-up evaporates when someone finds a better classical algorithm, which has happened repeatedly, or it depends on assumptions about how you load the data that quietly give away the whole game. I spent a few years playing what I called the "dequantization" referee, and the track record for exponential speed-ups outside the structured, algebraic, or quantum-simulation regime is pretty bad.

So, to summarize: simulating quantum systems, yes, with high confidence. Breaking cryptography, yes. A handful of other structured mathematical problems, yes. Generic optimization and machine learning, I'd want to see the actual argument, and usually when I do, it doesn't hold up.

astra-6.text:
The clearest case is simulating quantum physics itself. That was Feynman’s original motivation: if you want to understand a molecule or a material, a classical computer can require an amount of work that grows exponentially with the number of particles. A quantum computer can represent and manipulate that quantum state much more directly. Of course, you still have to prepare the state and extract useful information, but this is the application where I have the most confidence.

The other famous example is Shor’s algorithm for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms, which would break much of the public-key cryptography we use today. There’s an important caveat: we haven’t proved that no fast classical factoring algorithm exists. So the speed-up is compared with the best classical algorithms we know, rather than an unconditional mathematical lower bound.

What we don’t expect is that a quantum computer will give an exponential speed-up for every problem, or even for every hard optimization problem. The advantage depends on finding particular structure that quantum interference can exploit.

sol-6.1.text:
The clearest example is simulating quantum physics itself. That was Feynman’s original motivation: if you want to understand a molecule, a material, or a quantum field theory, a quantum computer is a very natural tool. We have strong theoretical reasons to expect exponential advantages for some of those problems, although that doesn’t mean every chemistry calculation will become exponentially faster.

Then there’s Shor’s algorithm, for factoring integers and computing discrete logarithms. Those are enormously important because of their role in cryptography. We know quantum computers can solve them in polynomial time, whereas the best known classical algorithms take much longer. The qualification is that we haven’t proved that no efficient classical algorithm exists.

Where I’m much more cautious is with claims about optimization, machine learning, or solving NP-complete problems. There are quantum algorithms that offer advantages, but an exponential speed-up generally requires some special structure. Quantum computing doesn’t just let you try every possible answer in parallel and read out the right one. The hard part is arranging interference so that the answers you want become more likely and the others cancel out.
